newsitem.title: USA: Eaton sees operating issues hurt 2nd half.
newsitem.headline: Eaton sees operating issues hurt 2nd half.

text.p: Eaton Corp said on Monday it would not meet its expected level of performance in fiscal 1996 partly because operating issues were hurting its performance in the second half of the year.

Stephen Hardis, chairman and chief executive officer, said: "We are disappointed with Eaton's overall financial results during the past quarter...persistent operating issues at a few of our operations are having a disproportionate effect on our results during the second half of this year."
Eaton also said it would take between $40 and $45 million in restructuring costs this year, to improve performance.
In Eaton's largest business segment, Electrical and Electronic Controls, Hardis said activity levels were more mixed than last year.

"We have now overcome most of the transitional plant integration difficulties which have hurt performance over the past year but we remain disappointed by activity and profit levels of our Industrial Controls business," Hardis said.

Sales at the industrial controls division continued about four percent ahead of year ago levels, but Hardis said the company was taking specific actions to return the business to traditional operating performance levels.
In specialty controls, sales were off four percent from last year's levels due partly to the sharp downturn in demand for semiconductor capital equipment, the company said.
Hardis said Eaton did not expect a year-on-year improvement in sales at this division before about mid-1997.

"As the leading worldwide producer of ion implanters, we are clearly feeling the effects of the slowdown in our sales, which are off about 25 percent from the first two quarters," he said. But Hardis said he was encouraged by the stability in orders over the past two months.
Eaton said sales at its Truck Components unit were off 8 percent from last year and down 16 percent excluding CAPCO sales, due to a downturn in both North and Latin America.

"Operating results are well below what we had expected given our projection for a 20 to 25 percent downturn in the North American heavy truck market," Hardis said. "Overall results have been affected both by disappointing market conditions outside North America and by unexpected operating problems around the world."
He said the Latin American markets for heavy trucks and agricultural equipment were much weaker than anticipated.
